svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two retry defences an AWS SDK provides and the boundary each one has. At the top, the backoff formula: the delay equals a uniformly random value between zero and one, multiplied by the smaller of twenty thousand milliseconds and the base delay doubled for each retry. The base delay is 50 milliseconds for transient errors and 1,000 milliseconds for throttling errors, and no individual delay exceeds the 20 second cap, although with the default of three max attempts the cap is never reached. In the middle, the first defence, full jitter, which spreads retries uniformly across the backoff window rather than stacking them on one instant, illustrated by AWS's own example of a thousand clients receiving a 503 simultaneously and having their first retries distributed across a 50 millisecond window. Beside it, the second defence, the retry quota token bucket, with a capacity of 500 tokens, a cost of 14 tokens for a transient retry and 5 for a throttling retry, restoring 1 token when a request succeeds on the first attempt, and beginning to drain above roughly 22 percent sustained transient failures or 32 percent throttling failures. A panel across the bottom records the shared limitation: the token budget is scoped to a single SDK client instance and is not shared across processes or hosts, so a fleet holds one independent budget per client and nothing aggregates them, meaning jitter smooths the spike and the quota protects the individual caller while neither reduces total fleet load. A final note records that all of this behaviour is opt-in until it becomes default, requiring the environment variable AWS underscore NEW underscore RETRIES underscore 2026 set to true.
svg.title: Two defences, both scoped to a single client instance
svg.text: Both defences stop at the edge of one client
Jitter decides when a client retries. The budget decides whether it retries. Neither knows another client exists.
The whole backoff scheme is one line
delay = random(0, 1) × min(20,000 ms, base_delay × 2^retry)
base_delay: 50 ms transient · 1,000 ms throttling · cap 20 s — never reached at the default of 3 attempts
Defence 1 · Full jitter
Changes when the retry is sent.
“1,000 clients all receive a 503 at the same
moment… distributes their first retries
uniformly across a 50 ms window.”
A thousand requests still arrive.
The spike is smoothed; the volume is not.
Defence 2 · Retry quota
Changes whether the retry is sent.
capacity 500 tokens
transient retry −14
throttling retry − 5
first-try success + 1
Drains above ~22% transient, ~32% throttling.
The limitation they share
“The token budget is typically scoped to a single SDK client instance… It is not shared across processes or hosts.”
A thousand hosts hold a thousand full budgets, each discovering the outage privately. Nothing aggregates them.
And none of it is on by default yet
Requires AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026=true. Without it: pre-2026 backoff timing, quota costs and service-specific defaults.
Fleet-wide protection has to come from somewhere that can see the fleet — a server-side throttle, a queue, or an x-amz-retry-after the service picks.
